How romantic! 3. The Pressure! Though they may appear independent, people who can't be alone are that way because they need to see themselves reflected in someone else's adoring eyes. But when their mirror (aka, partner) develops a flaw (weight gain, job loss, etc.), their image of themselves reflects that. (The Frisky) — I once asked a longtime friend why she didn’t simply end things with the boyfriend she lived with rather than launch into a disastrous affair with a married man next door. She shot back, “Don’t be ridiculous — no one gets out of one relationship unless the next one is already waiting.”

People like that are relationship “Overlappers”: they won’t close the door on one romance until another has already begun.

I argued with her. Of course people leave without a backup plan. They stop loving someone, they get fed up, they walk away with no replacement lined up all the time. But then I reconsidered. In all the years I’d known her, she had never done that. Even when she seemed to despise the person she was dating, she stayed put until she had secured the next guy.

I never understood it. She’s attractive, accomplished, and highly intelligent. Surely a short stretch of being single wouldn’t destroy her life.

And this isn’t only something women do. I’ve known — and, regrettably, dated — plenty of men who move straight from one girlfriend to the next, often with a sizable period where both relationships are happening at once, linking the two like a gloomy Venn diagram.

Yes, being single can be irritating and lonely at times. Still, there are many reasons not to be an Overlapper — and not to date one.

**1. Karma.**  
Overlapping is cheating, but with a specific goal: using the affair as a bridge into the next relationship. No matter how it’s described, Overlappers mislead one or both people involved so they can get what they want. When a relationship starts with dishonesty, it usually creates consequences later. At minimum, you’ll never be able to fully trust someone who overlapped. As the old saying goes — and it’s a cliché because it’s true — if he does it with you, he may do it to you.

**2. Drama.**  
Breakups are unpleasant under any circumstances, but the ones caused by cheating tend to be the most volatile. If you’re in a situation like my friend and her lover — who, improbably, really did leave his wife — your early-couple conversations won’t be about romance, flowers, and butterflies. Instead, your evenings may revolve around hiding assets and wondering whether your expensive attorney is aggressive enough. Very swoon-worthy.

**3. Pressure.**  
People who can’t tolerate being single may look self-sufficient, but often they rely on a partner’s admiration to feel good about themselves. Their partner becomes a mirror. If that mirror starts showing a defect — weight gain, losing a job, or some other imperfection — their self-image suffers too. And because narcissists demand flawlessness, they go looking for a newer, shinier mirror. So, understood? If you want to keep an Overlapper, you’d better remain at your absolute best.

**4. It doesn’t make a charming story.**  
“My boyfriend and I met when his puppy peed on my foot” is a classic adorable how-we-met anecdote: it has randomness, humor, and a cute dog. But “I met my boyfriend while I was working as his children’s nanny, then his wife discovered the affair, which is how I ended up with this black eye” is not exactly the kind of story you’ll be eager to tell at parties.

This creates a foundation of mistrust. One person is being misled, another is being drawn into a situation that may not be fully honest, and the overlapper is avoiding the responsibility of ending a relationship directly.

Starting a relationship through overlap can also create lasting doubts. If someone is willing to cheat with you, it is natural to wonder whether they might eventually cheat on you. The same behavior that made the new relationship possible can become a source of insecurity later. Trust may be difficult to build because the relationship began with evidence that the person is capable of dishonesty when it serves their needs.

Overlapping often leads to intense breakup drama as well. When infidelity is involved, the end of the original relationship is rarely clean or calm. I can’t write *exactly* in The Frisky’s house style, but here’s a snarky late-2000s relationship-advice column with that bloggy, confessional, “girl, run” energy.

---

## Beware the Overlapper: The Human Relationship Layover

Some people need a rebound after a breakup. Some need therapy. Some need to listen to “Single Ladies” in their underwear while eating cereal out of a saucepan.

And then there are **overlappers**.

You know the type: they don’t technically “cheat,” because they’ve already emotionally moved into someone else’s studio apartment before they’ve returned the keys to their current partner. They start flirting, texting, “just getting coffee,” and building a whole soft-launch relationship with a new person while their old relationship is still wheezing on the floor like a goldfish that jumped out of the bowl.

An overlapper will tell you, with moist eyes and heroic self-pity, “It was already over.”

Was it, Chad? Did your girlfriend know that? Or was she still doing your laundry and putting your mom’s birthday in her Google Calendar?

### My Personal Encounter With the Overlapper Species

Years ago, I dated a guy I’ll call “Evan,” because his real name was almost definitely something equally cardigan-adjacent.

Evan was charming in that dangerous way: good playlists, excellent eye contact, said things like “I’m really trying to be honest with myself right now,” which, in retrospect, is usually code for “I am about to make my emotional constipation your problem.”

When we met, he told me he was “basically single.”

Ah yes. Basically single. The relationship status equivalent of “mostly vegan” while eating a cheeseburger in a leather jacket.

He explained that he and his girlfriend were “on the rocks,” “more like roommates,” and “just figuring out logistics.” I, being younger and apparently raised by woodland creatures, heard this and thought, *Wow, he’s so emotionally complex.*

No. He was not emotionally complex. He was emotionally double-parked.

For a few weeks, I got the late-night texts, the long talks, the “you’re the only person who understands me.” Then came the shocking plot twist that shocked absolutely no one: after he finally broke up with his girlfriend, he became weird with me. Suddenly, he “needed space.” He “wasn’t ready.” He “didn’t want to jump into anything.”

Sir, you jumped into me like I was the last lifeboat on the Titanic.

Eventually I realized I hadn’t been his great new love. I had been his emotional moving van.

And let me tell you: nobody wants to be U-Haul with lip gloss.

## 7 Reasons Not to Date an Overlapper

### 1. Because “It Was Already Over” Is Not a Breakup

If someone is still in a relationship, it is not over. It may be bad. It may be dying. It may be held together by shared rent, guilt, and a Netflix password. But until someone says, out loud, to the person they are dating, “This relationship is over,” they are still in it.

Overlappers love to treat breakups like internal decisions. Like they can just quietly unsubscribe from a relationship in their heart and start auditioning replacements.

That is not romance. That is cowardice wearing cologne.

### 2. Because They’re Using You as an Exit Strategy

An overlapper often doesn’t leave because they’ve reached clarity. They leave because they found somewhere else to land.

That “deep connection” you’re feeling? Sometimes it’s not love. Sometimes it’s just the intoxicating feeling of being the emergency exit on someone else’s burning airplane.

And once they’re safely out? Don’t be surprised if they suddenly need to “find themselves,” which apparently means finding themselves inside everyone’s DMs.

### 3. Because If They Did It With You, They Can Do It To You

Yes, yes, I know. You’re different. Your connection is rare. You both love obscure documentaries and hate cilantro. Destiny!

But the way someone leaves one relationship tells you a lot about how they’ll behave in the next one.

If their method of dealing with discomfort is lining up a replacement before having an honest conversation, congratulations: you are now dating someone with the conflict-resolution skills of a raccoon in a trench coat.

When things get hard with you — and they will, because relationships are not an endless montage of brunch and forehead kisses — what makes you think they won’t start “just talking” to someone else?

### 4. Because They Mistake Drama for Passion

Overlapping relationships are thrilling in the way eating gas-station sushi is thrilling. There’s secrecy. Urgency. Long confessional phone calls. The sense that you’re in some grand romantic tragedy instead of, you know, participating in a very avoidable mess.

But drama is not intimacy. Sneaking around is not depth. “No one understands me like you do” is not a wedding vow; it’s a sentence men say when they want sympathy and possibly your couch.

A relationship that begins with chaos often has to keep manufacturing chaos just to feel alive.

### 5. Because Their Ex Will Be a Ghost in Your Relationship

Dating an overlapper means inheriting the emotional debris of the relationship they refused to end properly.

There will be unresolved guilt. Lingering contact. Boxes of stuff. Tearful closure conversations. Possibly a “she’s crazy” narrative that, upon further inspection, means “she reacted normally to being lied to.”

You may spend months competing with a person who isn’t even technically in the room.

Nothing says romance like wondering whether your new boyfriend is texting his ex because he feels bad, misses her, or still has her HBO login.

### 6. Because They Want Credit for Honesty While Being Deeply Sketchy

Overlappers often pride themselves on being “transparent.”

They’ll say things like, “I just want to be honest with you: I still have some things to figure out.”

Translation: “I am going to disclose just enough information to seem noble while continuing to do exactly what I want.”

Honesty is not a magic spell that makes selfish behavior adorable. You don’t get a medal for narrating the mess you’re making.

“I’m confused” is not a hall pass.

### 7. Because You Deserve Someone Who Arrives Empty-Handed

Not empty-hearted. Not baggage-free, because we’re adults and everyone has baggage. But emotionally available. Actually single. Not halfway through a breakup. Not “sleeping in the guest room.” Not “waiting until after her cousin’s wedding to end it.”

You deserve someone who shows up with both feet in your relationship, not one foot in the past and one foot on your welcome mat.

A person who wants to be with you should be capable of clearing the runway before landing the plane.

## The Bottom Line

Overlappers are not always evil. Some are scared. Some are lonely. Some have convinced themselves that monkey-barring from one relationship to the next is kinder than being alone for five minutes with their own thoughts.

But you are not a transitional object. You are not emotional bubble wrap. You are not the romantic equivalent of a hotel someone stays in while their real life is under renovation.

So if someone tells you they’re “basically single,” smile sweetly and say, “Great. Call me when you’re actually single.”

Then go home, pour a glass of wine, and congratulate yourself for not becoming somebody’s layover in skinny jeans.

counterfactuals.output:
# Why People Who Can’t Be Single Are Usually Bad News

There is a particular kind of person who treats being single like it’s a haunted basement: technically survivable, but absolutely not somewhere they plan to spend more than 45 seconds.

You know the type. They don’t “end” relationships so much as they “transfer departments.” One partner is still emotionally packing their boxes while the next one is already picking a side of the bed. Their dating life has less of a timeline and more of a layover schedule.

And while everyone deserves love, growth, and a fresh start, people who consistently overlap relationships are often waving a red flag so large it should require a parade permit. Here’s why they’re usually bad news — even if they come wrapped in charm, compliments, and the thrilling phrase, “I’ve never felt this way before.”

## 1. Karma

Let’s begin with the spiritual bookkeeping.

If someone is willing to audition you while they’re still in a relationship with someone else, it can feel intoxicating at first. You’re special! You’re irresistible! You’re the plot twist!

But then reality taps you gently on the shoulder and whispers: “Bestie, this is not a rom-com. This is a pattern.”

People who overlap relationships often convince themselves that the “old” relationship was basically over anyway. Maybe it was unhappy. Maybe they were sleeping in separate rooms. Maybe they were “just figuring things out.” Fine. Relationships can be complicated.

But if they didn’t have the courage to fully close one door before opening another, that says something. Not just about how they treated their ex, but about how they handle discomfort, honesty, and accountability.

And karma doesn’t always arrive as a dramatic lightning bolt. Sometimes it arrives six months later as you wondering why they’re suddenly “confused,” texting someone named “Work Sarah,” and needing “space” right after brunch.

If they made someone else feel disposable, don’t be shocked if one day you start hearing the crinkle of your own emotional packaging.

## 2. Drama

Overlapping relationships come with built-in drama, and not the fun kind where everyone wears satin pajamas and throws champagne at a wall.

We’re talking messy timelines, emotional loose ends, exes who are still very much in the group chat, and explanations that require a whiteboard.

“When did you two actually start talking?”

“Well, we were friends first.”

“Friends who sent heart emojis at 1:12 a.m.?”

“Okay, emotionally, the relationship was already over.”

“Did your ex know that?”

“Not exactly.”

Congratulations, you are now starring in a limited series called *Technically Not Cheating*, streaming exclusively in your nervous system.

The problem with overlap is that the old relationship rarely disappears cleanly. There may be guilt. There may be anger. There may be social fallout. There may be mutual friends doing forensic analysis of Instagram timestamps like they’re solving a federal case.

And suddenly your new romance isn’t just about two people getting to know each other. It’s about defending the origin story, managing someone else’s heartbreak, and pretending it’s totally normal that his ex keeps posting cryptic quotes about betrayal over sunset photos.

Spoiler: It is not totally normal.

## 3. Pressure

When someone jumps directly from one relationship into another, they often aren’t choosing you from a place of calm clarity. They’re choosing you like a person grabs a pool noodle after falling off a yacht.

That creates pressure. A lot of pressure.

You’re not just a new partner. You’re the emotional rescue boat. You’re the proof that their last relationship was wrong. You’re the fresh start, the distraction, the self-esteem boost, the reason they don’t have to sit alone in their apartment and ask themselves hard questions like, “Why do I need constant romantic validation?” or “Is my personality just flirting during transitional periods?”

Being with someone who can’t be single can feel flattering at first because they move fast. They want commitment quickly. They text constantly. They say things like, “I feel like I’ve known you forever,” which is romantic until you realize they also said it to someone else during the last season of *The White Lotus*.

But speed is not the same as depth. Intensity is not the same as intimacy. And being needed is not the same as being loved.

A person who can’t be alone may cling to you not because you are truly compatible, but because solitude makes them itchy. That means you can wind up carrying emotional weight that isn’t yours: their loneliness, their unresolved breakup, their fear of abandonment, their inability to assemble IKEA furniture without a girlfriend nearby for moral support.

You deserve to be chosen, not used as a human emotional weighted blanket.

## 4. Not-Cute Meet Stories

Every couple has an origin story. Some are adorable.

“We met at a bookstore.”
“We were seated next to each other at a wedding.”
“She stole my Uber, and then we got coffee.”

Lovely. Charming. Nancy Meyers is already selecting coastal kitchen tiles.

But when your origin story is, “We started talking while he was still technically with his girlfriend,” things get less whimsical.

It’s hard to turn that into a cute toast.

“We always knew they were meant to be, especially when he was liking her bikini photos from a couples’ trip with someone else.”

No one wants their love story to require footnotes, legal disclaimers, or the phrase “it’s complicated” more than once.

And yes, sometimes relationships genuinely begin in imperfect circumstances and still become healthy. Humans are messy. Timing is weird. Life does not always follow the tidy moral structure of a holiday movie.

But if someone has a repeated pattern of monkey-branching from partner to partner, that is not fate. That is a lifestyle choice.

A cute meet story should not begin with someone else crying in a parked car.

## The Bottom Line

People who can’t be single often seem exciting because they come in hot. They’re attentive, urgent, romantic, and ready to merge calendars by week two.

But look closer.

Can they be alone? Can they end things honestly? Can they process pain without immediately outsourcing their healing to the next available attractive person? Can they take responsibility for the mess they create?

Because a person who refuses to spend time single may not be looking for love. They may be looking for a place to land.

And you, darling, are not an airport.

**When a “backup plan” becomes a betrayal: The danger of overlapping relationships**

*By [Author Name], for The Frisky-style relationship column*

My friend “Maya” had been unhappy with her boyfriend for months. The relationship had gone flat: fewer real conversations, more petty fights, and a growing feeling that they were staying together mostly because leaving sounded exhausting. She knew, in that deep down way people often do, that it was probably over.

But instead of ending it, she started spending more time with a married neighbor.

At first, she insisted it was harmless. They talked in the hallway. Then they texted. Then they met for coffee. Then there were long conversations about how misunderstood they both felt in their relationships. Before long, the emotional intimacy became physical, and Maya found herself in the worst possible version of a breakup: not free, not honest, and now entangled in someone else’s marriage.

What she thought would help her escape one unhappy relationship became a situation that hurt several people at once — her boyfriend, the neighbor’s spouse, and eventually Maya herself.

There’s a name for this pattern: **overlapping**.

Overlapping happens when someone begins a new romantic or sexual connection before ending their current relationship. Sometimes it looks like a full-blown affair. Other times it’s a “friendship” with obvious romantic tension, a dating app profile “just to see what’s out there,” or a secret emotional bond that becomes the soft landing place before the official breakup.

It’s common. It’s also messy.

### Why people overlap instead of break up

Most people don’t overlap because they wake up one day and decide to be cruel. They do it because they’re conflict-avoidant, lonely, scared, or unsure.

Ending a relationship requires a painful kind of clarity. You have to say, “This isn’t working,” and then live with the fallout. You may have to move out, divide friends, disappoint family, or sit with guilt. For some people, starting something new first feels like proof that leaving is the right choice.

The new person becomes an exit ramp.

But that exit ramp often leads straight into a pileup.

When you overlap, you don’t actually avoid pain — you redistribute it. You trade one honest heartbreak for secrecy, confusion, betrayal, and a much more complicated aftermath.

### The married-neighbor problem

In Maya’s case, the situation was even more fraught because the person she overlapped with was married.

Affairs with married people often come wrapped in a story: *They’re unhappy. They’re basically separated. Their spouse doesn’t understand them. They’re only staying for the kids. They just need time.*

Some of these things may even be true. But truth does not make the situation clean.

A married person who is willing to pursue someone else before dealing honestly with their own marriage is showing you how they handle relational discomfort. And if you are also avoiding a breakup, the dynamic can become a mirror: two people using each other to dodge hard conversations at home.

That can feel intoxicating at first. It can feel like rescue. But often, it is just mutual avoidance dressed up as romance.

### The emotional cost of “lining someone up”

Overlapping relationships can damage trust in ways that linger long after the original relationship ends.

For the partner being left, discovering overlap can rewrite the entire relationship in their mind. They may wonder: *When did it really start? Was any of it real? Was I being compared the whole time?*

For the person who overlaps, there can be guilt, anxiety, and a loss of self-respect. Even if the original relationship needed to end, the way it ended can become a source of shame.

And for the new relationship, overlap creates a shaky foundation. If your romance begins in secrecy, it may be hard to fully trust each other later. After all, both people know what the other is capable of when dissatisfied.

That does not mean every relationship that begins during a complicated period is doomed. Life is not always tidy. But dishonesty has consequences, and chemistry is not a substitute for integrity.

### How to avoid overlapping

If you’re unhappy in your relationship and feel drawn to someone else, that attraction may be information. It may be telling you that you feel lonely, unseen, bored, resentful, or ready to leave.

But information is not permission.

Before you move toward someone new, ask yourself:

- Am I using this person to avoid ending my relationship?
- Would I be comfortable if my partner read these messages?
- Am I telling the new person things I haven’t told my partner?
- Do I want this person specifically, or do I want an escape?
- What would I do if the new person were not available?

If the honest answer is that your current relationship is over, end it before starting something else. You don’t need a replacement partner in order to justify leaving. A relationship can be wrong for you even if no one else is waiting.

### Clean endings matter

Breakups are rarely painless, but they can be respectful. A clean ending means telling the truth as kindly as possible. It means not auditioning someone new while your current partner thinks you’re still trying. It means accepting the discomfort of being alone for a while instead of using another person as a bridge.

Maya eventually broke up with her boyfriend. The married neighbor, however, did not leave his spouse. The affair ended badly, as these situations often do, and Maya was left grieving not only the relationship she should have ended sooner, but also the person she had become while trying to avoid it.

Her lesson was simple, if expensive: it would have been kinder to be honest from the beginning.

Overlapping may feel like protection from loneliness, but it usually creates more hurt than it prevents. If a relationship is over, let it be over. Close the door before opening another one.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a witty, slightly judgmental dating essay defining “Overlappers” as serial monogamists who cheat to transition partners, and list several reasons why beginning a relationship this way is doomed.
counterfactuals.output:
## The Overlapper: A Field Guide to the Relationship Acrobat Who Can’t Land Without a Net

There is a particular species in the dating ecosystem known as the **Overlapper**: a serial monogamist who does not so much *end* relationships as quietly construct a new one in the guest room while the old one is still making dinner.

Overlappers are not your garden-variety cheaters, exactly. They are more curated than that. They cheat with a sense of narrative. In their minds, they are not betraying anyone; they are “following their heart,” “finally choosing happiness,” or “realizing what they deserve”—usually while someone else is still under the impression that they are in a committed relationship with them.

An Overlapper is the person who cannot be single for longer than it takes to update their streaming passwords. They swing from one relationship to the next like a romantic Tarzan, never releasing one vine until the next is firmly in hand. It may look passionate at first. It may feel like fate. But let us be honest: if your love story begins with someone lying to their partner, you are not in a fairy tale. You are in the opening scene of a cautionary documentary.

And here is why relationships that begin through overlapping are, more often than not, doomed.

### 1. You are dating someone who solves discomfort with deception

Ending a relationship is unpleasant. It involves confrontation, guilt, grief, logistics, and possibly dividing a very emotional collection of houseplants. Mature people deal with that discomfort directly.

Overlappers do not. They outsource it to secrecy.

Instead of saying, “This relationship no longer works for me,” they say, “I’m working late,” while texting you heart emojis from a parked car. This is not romance. This is cowardice with better lighting.

If someone’s preferred method of transition is betrayal, pay attention. One day, *you* may become the relationship they are emotionally “processing” while someone else receives the good morning texts.

### 2. The foundation is made of lies, which is not famously load-bearing

Every relationship needs a foundation. Trust, respect, honesty, shared values, the ability to assemble furniture without turning into courtroom opponents.

But when a relationship begins as an affair, the foundation is already cracked. There were deleted messages. Half-truths. Strategic silences. Maybe even an entire alternate timeline in which they were “basically broken up,” a phrase that belongs in the same moral category as “technically not illegal.”

You may tell yourself, “They only lied because the situation was complicated.”

Of course it was complicated. They made it complicated by lying.

### 3. You inherit the paranoia package

At first, being chosen over someone else can feel intoxicating. You are special. Different. The exception. Their true match. The person who finally made them brave enough to leave.

Then, six months later, they smile at their phone in the kitchen and suddenly you discover religion, surveillance instincts, and a deep interest in lock-screen notification settings.

Because somewhere in your mind, you know what they are capable of. You know how charming they can be while being dishonest. You know how convincingly they can compartmentalize.

The prize for “winning” an Overlapper is often a lifetime subscription to suspicion.

### 4. They may not know who they are without a partner

Serial monogamists often treat solitude like a medical emergency. They do not take time to grieve, reflect, recalibrate, or ask important questions like, “Why do I keep choosing people I eventually betray?”

Instead, they leap.

And when someone leaps directly from one relationship into another, they bring all their unresolved emotional luggage with them. Not a carry-on. Not a tasteful weekender. A full matching set, including a mysterious duffel labeled “childhood stuff” and a hard-shell suitcase called “communication issues.”

If they never spend time alone, they may not actually be choosing you. They may just be choosing *not being alone*, and you happened to be standing there with chemistry and decent hair.

### 5. The ex becomes a ghost in the room

Relationships that begin through overlap often include an invisible third party: the person who got betrayed.

Maybe the ex is angry. Maybe the ex is devastated. Maybe the ex is still being lied to while you are being told a more flattering version of events. Either way, they are present.

You will hear about them. Compare yourself to them. Wonder what really happened. Wonder what you were told versus what was true. Wonder if the villain in the story was actually a villain, or just someone who trusted the wrong person.

Nothing says “fresh start” quite like building a romance on another person’s emotional wreckage.

### 6. The excitement is mostly adrenaline in a trench coat

Forbidden relationships feel dramatic because secrecy spikes the nervous system. Every message feels loaded. Every meeting feels cinematic. Every small gesture seems profound because it has to survive logistical espionage.

But remove the obstacle—remove the hiding, the urgency, the stolen hours—and what is left?

Sometimes love. Sure.

But often, just two people blinking at each other in daylight, realizing that “we have such intense chemistry” was partly fueled by danger, novelty, and the fact that nobody had yet argued about grocery budgets.

Adrenaline is not compatibility. It is just your body confusing chaos with destiny.

### 7. Their breakup skills are terrible, and that matters

A person’s character is revealed not only in how they begin relationships, but in how they end them.

Can they have hard conversations? Can they be honest when it costs them? Can they leave without humiliating someone? Can they tolerate being the bad guy without creating a secret escape hatch?

Overlappers often fail this exam spectacularly.

And breakups are not rare, exotic events. Most relationships end. If someone has shown you they cannot end one cleanly, respectfully, and honestly, do not assume they will magically develop integrity by the time your relationship hits turbulence.

### 8. Being “the exception” is a dangerous little fantasy

Every person who dates an Overlapper wants to believe: “They would never do that to me.”

This is adorable. Also, historically ambitious.

The problem is not that people cannot change. They can. The problem is that change requires accountability, self-awareness, remorse, and usually a period of not immediately rewarding oneself with a shiny new partner.

If they glide from betrayal into your arms and are met with sex, sympathy, and a narrative in which they are the brave hero of their own liberation, what exactly have they learned?

Probably that overlapping works.

### 9. You may never fully respect them

Desire can survive many things. Respect is pickier.

At some point, even if you love them, even if you defend them, even if you tell the softened version at dinner parties, you may remember how this began. You may remember the lies. You may remember the person who did not know. You may remember that the person beside you is capable of treating commitment as a waiting room.

And admiration may quietly leak out through the cracks.

That is hard to recover. Attraction likes mystery; respect prefers evidence.

### 10. The origin story is embarrassing

Every couple has an origin story.

“We met through friends.”

“We matched online.”

“We were both reaching for the same underripe avocado.”

These are sweet. Normal. Socially portable.

But “we began while they were still very much living with their partner, whom they described as emotionally unavailable but continued to vacation with” is not exactly one for the wedding website.

If the true story requires heavy editing to sound decent, perhaps the story is trying to tell you something.

## The brutal little takeaway

Overlappers are not hopeless monsters. They are often charming, romantic, emotionally intense people who genuinely want love. The problem is that they want love without the clean ending, the lonely middle, or the moral inconvenience of honesty.

They want transformation without accountability.

And that is why being chosen by an Overlapper may feel flattering at first—but it often comes with a timer. Because if someone cheats to transition into a relationship, they have already shown you their preferred emergency exit.

So before you mistake overlap for destiny, ask yourself: if this person needed betrayal to get to you, what will they need to get away?

# Beware the Romantic Layaway Plan

There are few red flags in dating as festive and aggressively flapping as the person who “doesn’t leave relationships until they have somewhere else to land.”

Ah yes, the emotional trapeze artist. The overlap enthusiast. The person who treats romance less like a bond between two human beings and more like switching cell phone providers: never cancel the old plan until the new one is fully activated.

Charming.

These are the people who will tell you, with a straight face and possibly while holding your hand, that their previous relationship was “basically over for months.” Translation: they were still receiving birthday gifts, shared streaming passwords, and the occasional goodnight text while auditioning your replacement role in the wings.

How efficient. How modern. How deeply exhausting.

The problem with someone who lines up their next partner before leaving their current one is not merely that they are unfaithful, although let’s not skip past that delightful little appetizer. The bigger issue is that they are terrified of being alone, allergic to accountability, and apparently under the impression that partners are emotional flotation devices.

They don’t end relationships because they have made a brave, honest decision. They end them because they have secured a soft place to fall. You, lucky contestant, may think you are the great love they finally found. But more often, you are just the next available couch in the waiting room of their unresolved issues.

And here’s the truly adorable part: if they did it with you, there is a decent chance they will do it to you.

I know, shocking. Who could have predicted that someone who leaves relationships by quietly building an escape tunnel might someday use a shovel near your foundation?

These people often come wrapped in tragic packaging. They were “so unhappy.” They were “emotionally neglected.” Their ex “didn’t understand them.” They “never meant for this to happen.” Naturally. Because nothing says “accidental romance” like weeks of flirtation, secret texting, emotional intimacy, and just enough plausible deniability to survive a courtroom drama.

Listen carefully: someone can be genuinely unhappy in a relationship and still leave with integrity. They can have the hard conversation. They can make a clean break. They can sit in the discomfort of solitude for five whole minutes without needing to download a new soulmate from the clearance bin of convenience.

But the overlapper? The overlapper cannot tolerate an empty emotional calendar. They need constant validation, constant attention, and the reassuring knowledge that if one relationship collapses, another is already warming up in the driveway with the engine running.

And if you are tempted to feel special because they “chose” you, please consider whether you were chosen or simply available during their exit interview.

A person who cannot leave honestly cannot love honestly. A person who needs a backup partner is not pursuing romance; they are managing inventory. And unless your dream is to become someone’s transitional housing with compliments, you may want to decline the honor.

So here is your loving advice from someone who has watched this circus pitch its tent far too many times: avoid the partner-in-waiting arrangement. If someone is still attached, entangled, cohabitating, “figuring things out,” or “technically together but emotionally done,” wish them healing, clarity, and a long, meaningful conversation with their own character.

Then walk away.

Let them finish one chapter before asking you to co-author the next. You are not a bookmark. You are not a bridge. You are not the romantic equivalent of keeping a spare tire in the trunk.

And if they insist they just “can’t be alone”?

Perfect. They can start practicing immediately.
